article.title: Why Feature Stores Need Point-in-Time Correct Joins
article.why: 避免特徵工程把預測時點之後的資訊洩漏進模型。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Machine-learning datasets often look correct while quietly containing information from the future. This problem is called data leakage. One common source is a join that uses the latest version of a table instead of the version that would have been available at the moment a prediction was made.

Imagine building a model to predict on June 1 whether a customer will cancel during the next month. Your feature table contains “current customer status.” If you build training data in August by joining June records to the latest customer table, the status field may already say that the customer cancelled on June 20. The model is then allowed to learn from an event that had not happened on June 1.

A point-in-time correct join prevents this. For each training observation, every feature must reflect information available at or before that observation's prediction timestamp. Instead of asking, “What is this customer's status now?” the pipeline asks, “What was the latest known status as of June 1?”

This requirement becomes difficult when source systems update records in place. A table may store only the newest address, account status, or category. Once the value changes, the old state disappears. In that case, a feature platform cannot reconstruct history reliably unless upstream systems preserve change history, snapshots, event logs, or effective timestamps.

Two kinds of time are often relevant. Event time describes when something happened in the real world. Processing or ingestion time describes when the system learned about it. A transaction may occur on May 30 but arrive on June 2. For a prediction made June 1, using that transaction may still be leakage if the production system could not have known it yet.

Aggregations need the same discipline. A “30-day purchase count” for a June 1 prediction should include only eligible events from the defined lookback window and only data available by the prediction cutoff. Accidentally calculating the feature from a table refreshed after the outcome period can create excellent offline metrics and disappointing production performance.

Feature stores can help by standardizing historical retrieval, but a feature store does not magically make data correct. Teams still need explicit entity keys, timestamps, freshness rules, late-arriving-data policies, and definitions for how features are reconstructed. The training pipeline and online serving logic should implement compatible semantics.

Testing should include temporal checks, not only schema checks. Sample training rows and manually reconstruct what was knowable at their prediction times. Compare offline feature values with archived production values when possible. Add automated assertions that feature timestamps do not exceed prediction timestamps, while remembering that a valid timestamp alone does not prove the information was actually available.

The business impact can be severe. Leakage makes a model look more accurate during validation, encouraging deployment or investment based on unrealistic performance. It can also distort feature importance and lead teams to optimize signals that disappear in production.

A useful rule is to imagine replaying history. Freeze the clock at each prediction time and ask whether the pipeline could have produced exactly the same feature vector using only information that existed then. If the answer is no, the dataset is not a faithful simulation of the prediction problem. Point-in-time correctness is therefore not merely a data-engineering detail; it is part of the definition of a valid machine-learning experiment.

The safest workflow treats every feature as a time-bounded claim. Document when its source event occurred, when it became observable, and which timestamp the training join uses. This makes leakage reviews concrete and helps data scientists and engineers reason about the same production reality.
